opening_message:
Ticket 1: Eric Woods (employee ID E019) requests write access to Payroll.

Team memory: 2 note(s) about employee E019.
Note 1 (ticket 1):
  - role: Engineer (looked up in own database before writing)
  - employment type: full_time (looked up in own database before writing)
  - recommendation for Payroll: write
  - comment: Eric Woods (E019) is a full-time Engineer requesting write access to Payroll. As full-time employee, maximum is write (admin only for role-owned systems, and Payroll is owned by Payroll Specialist). Requested level (write) equals the maximum, so recommend write.
Note 2 (ticket 1):
  - role: Engineer (not looked up in own database before writing; same value as note 1)
  - employment type: contractor (looked up in own database before writing)
  - security training: basic (looked up in own database before writing)
  - recommendation for Payroll: read
  - comment: Security DB shows Eric Woods (E019) is a contractor with basic security training. Contractors max is read unless they have advanced training (never admin). Requested write exceeds the max, so recommend read.
reason: The two team notes conflict on Eric Woods' (E019) employment status: the HR note says full-time (max write for Payroll, recommend write), while the Security note says contractor with basic security training (max read, recommend read). Because the facts conflict and the employee's role (Engineer) does not own Payroll, I grant the more restrictive supported level, read, to avoid granting write in case the contractor status holds. Requested write exceeds that, so read is granted.

1. full_time employees: up to write. Admin only if role owns system. Engineer doesn't own Payroll, so max write.
2. contractor: read, or write if advanced security training. Never admin.

If full-time: requested write = max write → grant write.
If contractor with basic training: max is read → grant read.
